openers.neoarchean-era: The Neoarchean is the age of supervolcanoes and stitched-together continents. In Ontario and Quebec the Abitibi greenstone belt formed, home to the Blake River Megacaldera Complex, the first known Precambrian supervolcano, and around 2,705 million years ago a possibly global eruption of komatiite lava may mark an overturn of the mantle. Cratons welded together: the Kaapvaal and Zimbabwe along the Limpopo Belt, and many more into the hypothetical supercontinent Kenorland. Meanwhile, about 2,700 million years ago, another pulse of oxygen hinted at the great change to come.

reviews.mesoarchean-era: The Mesoarchean is when the machinery of the modern Earth started to turn. Cyanobacteria began splitting water and releasing oxygen, enough for a brief rise around 2,980–2,960 million years ago, and the Pongola ice spread across a world otherwise kept warm by methane and carbon dioxide. Beneath them, continental crust grew fast, the first signs of modern-style subduction appeared in the Pilbara, and cratons such as the North Atlantic and Yilgarn assembled, perhaps into Ur. Rivers in the Witwatersrand Basin meanwhile gathered the gold that still makes it the world's richest field, while impact structures like Miralga and Maniitsoq remain fiercely argued over.

arch-035.title: The Saamian orogeny builds Fennoscandia's core
arch-035.text: The heart of a future supercontinent was forged in what is now northern Europe. Between 3.1 and 2.9 billion years ago, the Saamian orogeny built a wide area of tonalitic-trondhjemitic crust, light granite-like rock, in Fennoscandia. Gneiss and greenstone belts of the Baltic Shield were laid down in the Kola Peninsula, Karelia and northeastern Finland around 3,100 million years ago. This crust later formed the core of {{ref:arch-052}}.

arch-037.title: Miralga, an impact crater of disputed age
arch-037.text:
One crater has been given three very different ages in two years. Shatter cones, cone-shaped fractures made by an impact's shock wave, near Marble Bar in the Pilbara reveal the Miralga, or North Pole Dome, impact structure. Its crater may have exceeded 100 km.

A March 2025 study dated it to 3,470 ± 2 million years, which would make it the oldest known impact structure by over a billion years. A July 2025 study found shatter cones in rocks younger than 2.71 billion years, so the impact came after then and before 400 million years ago. A 2026 study dated impact-recrystallized zircon to 3.024 billion years and hydrothermal apatite to 3.019 billion. The age remains disputed.

arch-038.title: Maniitsoq, a doubtful impact in Greenland
arch-038.text: Not every round structure is a crater. One at Maniitsoq, West Greenland, was proposed as an ancient impact site, with an age refined to 3000.9 ± 1.9 million years. The impact evidence is highly contentious. Ultramafic intrusions there formed at 3013 million years ago, too old to have been made by the supposed impact, which argues against the idea.

arch-039.title: When did plate tectonics begin?
arch-039.text:
The ground beneath your feet moves a few centimeters a year, but when did it start moving? A possible onset of plate tectonics is placed around 3 billion years ago, yet its timing is still debated.

The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of modern-style subduction, where one plate dives beneath another. It includes an oceanic arc, a chain of volcanoes over a sinking plate, at a Pilbara convergent margin about 3.12 billion years ago. Diamonds add more clues. Minerals trapped in them suggest the supercontinent cycle, the repeated gathering and breakup of continents, began roughly 3 billion years ago, and diamonds from crustal eclogite became common after 3.0 billion.

Earlier, the picture differs. A hotter Paleoarchean mantle ruled out modern plate tectonics, and some suggest a stagnant lid, a single unbroken shell, instead. Other estimates range from the Hadean, over 4 billion years ago, to 2.2 billion years, or just 800 million years for fully modern-style tectonics. The debate links back to {{ref:hade-004}}.

arch-040.title: Continental crust grows fast
arch-040.text:
Before 3.7 billion years ago, continents held under 10% of today's continental crust. Then they grew quickly. There is little evidence of continental crust before 3.5 billion years ago, but roughly 20–25% of today's crust existed by 3.0 billion. After rapid crustal evolution, it reached about 60% by 2.6 billion years ago, with widespread mantle melting on the shields between 3.0 and 2.5 billion.

Much of the new crust was TTG rock, formed when water-rich mafic rock partly melted at high pressure. Whether subduction drove that melting is debated. The remaining fifth of the continental crust formed only during the last 2.5 billion years.

arch-041.title: The Pongola glaciation, Earth's first known ice age
arch-041.text:
In a warm Archean world, ice suddenly appears in the rocks of southern Africa. The Pongola glaciation, from about 2.985 to 2.837 billion years ago, is the oldest known glaciation on Earth.

Its traces are diamictites, jumbled mixtures of boulders and mud dropped by glaciers, in the Mozaan Formation of the Pongola Supergroup. They crop out in KwaZulu-Natal and Eswatini.

The cold was an interruption. The Mesoarchean climate was otherwise warm or temperate, kept mild by high methane and carbon dioxide, as in {{ref:arch-033}}. Ice reached a palaeolatitude, an ancient latitude, of 48 degrees. Whether it pushed further toward the tropics is uncertain.

What cooled the planet? Sulfur-isotope changes suggest a link to an early, short-lived oxygenation of the atmosphere, described in {{ref:arch-042}}. Oxygen reacts with methane, so a burst of it could have weakened the greenhouse that kept the Archean warm.

arch-042.title: Oxygen's first brief rise
arch-042.text: Oxygen made a short, early appearance long before it came to stay. A transient episode of higher oxygen occurred around 2,980–2,960 million years ago, in an atmosphere that otherwise had almost no free oxygen. By the Mesoarchean, oases of relatively high oxygen already existed in some nearshore shallow seas, around the cyanobacteria making it. Sulfur isotopes link this episode to the Pongola glaciation of the same age.

arch-043.title: The Witwatersrand Basin gathers its gold
arch-043.text: More gold has come out of one South African basin than anywhere else on Earth: over 40,000 tonnes mined, about 22% of all gold above ground. From about 2.97 to 2.71 billion years ago, rivers and a sea laid 5–7 km of mostly sedimentary rock in the Witwatersrand Basin on the Kaapvaal craton. As uplift pushed the sea back, braided river deltas on a wide coastal plain concentrated heavy minerals there: gold, pyrite and uraninite.

arch-044.title: The North Atlantic Craton assembles
arch-044.text: Rocks in Greenland, Labrador and Scotland were once one block. That block is the North Atlantic Craton, which grew as terranes collided in a series of orogenies. The Akia, Isukasia and Kapisilik terranes collided about 2950 million years ago. More terranes merged between 2850 and 2700 million years ago, and around Nuuk between 2650 and 2580 million. Regional magmatism, deformation and metamorphism then reworked and stabilized the craton.

arch-045.title: The Yilgarn Craton and its gold
arch-045.text: Western Australia's goldfields sit on a craton built from many pieces. The Yilgarn Craton was assembled between about 2.94 and 2.63 billion years ago from many terranes of older crust, mostly formed 3.2–2.8 billion years ago. Its bedrock includes the Narryer Gneiss, home of the {{ref:hade-011}}, beneath greenstone belts of about 2.70–2.55 billion years. Most of its gold was deposited 2650–2630 million years ago, after an earlier gold event at 2660–2655 million as the crust stretched.

arch-046.title: The Abitibi greenstone belt
arch-046.text: One of the world's largest Archean greenstone belts stretches across Ontario and Quebec. The Abitibi belt formed between 2,800 and 2,600 million years ago. It is mostly volcanic, a stack of thrusted slices like those of paired volcanic arcs and back-arc basins, with intrusions of 2,675–2,700 million years throughout. It contains the huge 2,707–2,696-million-year-old {{ref:arch-054}}.

arch-047.title: The Limpopo Belt welds two cratons
arch-047.text: A 250 km wide seam of crumpled rock joins two of Africa's oldest cratons. Late Archean metamorphism welded the Kaapvaal and Zimbabwe cratons along the Limpopo Belt about 2.8–2.5 billion years ago. High-pressure granulites, rocks cooked deep in the crust, formed in the belt about 2.69 billion years ago. Once the two cratons were stabilized together, the high-grade metamorphism in the belt ceased.

arch-048.title: North China's ancient basement forms
arch-048.text: Most of the deep rock under northern China dates from a single era. Neoarchean crust makes up 85% of the North China Craton's basement and formed in two pulses, 2.8–2.7 and 2.6–2.5 billion years ago. Banded iron formations and schists were laid down after the Fupingian orogeny of 2550 million years ago. Whether the craton's blocks joined about 2.5 billion years ago, in Kusky's model, or only at 1.85 billion, in Zhao's, is debated.

arch-049.title: The Fortescue and Hamersley basins fill
arch-049.text: Some of Australia's famous iron country began as a long-lived basin. From about 2.78 to 2.42 billion years ago, a thick pile of sedimentary and volcanic rock filled the Fortescue, Hamersley and Turee Creek basins on the Pilbara. Uranium–lead dating puts the base of this pile, the Mount Bruce Supergroup, at 2768 ± 16 million years. The Hamersley Basin was the last stable marine and river setting between the Yilgarn and Pilbara before rifting split them.

arch-050.title: The Slave Craton gains its deep root
arch-050.text: Canada's diamond mines tap the deep keel of the Slave Craton. Its main stabilization came about 2.75 billion years ago, marked by abundant peridotite, a dense mantle rock, in its root. Kaapvaal shows a similar growth peak, suggesting much of Earth's continental lithospheric mantle formed in the Neoarchean. Diamonds from craton roots are often over 3 billion years old, and the Slave's oldest, 3.5–3.3 billion years, imply a thick root far earlier.

arch-051.title: Tumbiana lakes and their puzzling microfossils
arch-051.text: The oldest known lakes rich in carbonate held life that is hard to classify. Western Australia's Tumbiana Formation, about 2727–2715 million years old, was laid down in such a lake system. Its limestones hold stromatolites such as Alcheringa narrina and organic-walled microfossils. Their size and protrusions resemble eukaryotic microbes, cells with a nucleus, but such features are not unique to eukaryotes, so what they were remains obscure.

arch-052.title: Kenorland, a possible supercontinent
arch-052.text:
Around 2.72 billion years ago, the scattered cratons may have gathered into a single landmass. Kenorland is a hypothetical supercontinent formed by the accretion of Neoarchean cratons and new continental crust. Its core was the Baltic, or Fennoscandian, Shield, traced back over 3.1 billion years, and {{ref:arch-065}} formed part of it. Its final assembly was finished by 2,600–2,550 million years ago, with the Superior and Wyoming provinces side by side.

It broke up sometime after 2.45–2.1 billion years ago, into proto-continents including Laurentia, Baltica, the Yilgarn and Kalahari. Not everyone accepts it. Alternatively, the cratons formed separate supercratons, Superia and Sclavia; the Slave collided with Sclavia by 2.6 billion years ago, and Superia's final assembly came at 2520 million.

arch-053.title: Ventersdorp lavas bury the gold fields
arch-053.text: A flood of lava sealed the Witwatersrand's gold beneath it. Massive outpourings, the Ventersdorp lavas, erupted about 2.715 billion years ago and abruptly ended deposition of the gold-rich Central Rand Group. Their cause is speculative: one source links them to the Kaapvaal craton's collision with the Zimbabwe Craton, another places them in a phase of rifting. The lavas and the Transvaal Supergroup above them were later warped into rings by the Vredefort impact.

arch-054.title: The Blake River supervolcano
arch-054.text: The first known Precambrian supervolcano rose in what is now Ontario and Quebec. The Blake River Megacaldera Complex began forming about 2,707 million years ago. Its first caldera, Misema, is 80 km long and 40 km wide, built from at least two merging mafic shield volcanoes. Later phases built the New Senator Caldera, 2704–2701 million years ago, and the Noranda Caldera, 2696 million years ago, piling up 7–9 km of erupted rock.

arch-055.title: Komatiite floods and a mantle overturn
arch-055.text: The hottest lavas in Earth's history erupted almost only in the Archean. Komatiite magma forms when 30–40% of mantle rock melts at very high pressure, and its lavas erupted at up to about 1600 °C. The mantle then may have been 100–250 °C hotter than now. Around 2,705 million years ago, a major and possibly global komatiite eruption occurred, and it may mark an overturn of the mantle.

arch-058.title: Another pulse of oxygen
arch-058.text:
Oxygen crept upward again about 2,700 million years ago. Skewed sulfur isotopes in pyrites, crystals of iron sulfide, show a small rise in atmospheric oxygen around this time. Cyanobacteria had appeared by at least 2.7 billion years ago, and an atmosphere containing oxygen began to develop in the late Archean.

Some consider this pulse a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event, the first lasting rise of oxygen in the air. Most scholars still place that start later, in the Paleoproterozoic, about 2,400 million years ago.

arch-059.title: The Stillwater complex, a layered treasure chest
arch-059.text: Montana's Beartooth Mountains expose a slice through a frozen magma chamber. The Stillwater complex, a large layered mafic intrusion, was injected into older gneisses about 2.7 billion years ago, and its minerals settled out in layers as it cooled. About 5,500 m of those layers are exposed along 48 km of the range. It holds large reserves of chromium and platinum-group metals such as palladium, and it resembles South Africa's Bushveld complex.

arch-060.title: Stromatolite reefs spread
arch-060.text: Microbes built the world's first reefs. Stromatolites occur throughout the Archean, but from about 2,700 million years ago they became a major part of the fossil record, and they grew common late in the eon. The earliest of confirmed microbial origin is 2.724 billion years old. In Zimbabwe, stromatolites of the Bulawayo series formed the first verified reef community on Earth.

arch-061.title: Sturgeon Lake Caldera
arch-061.text: A collapsed volcano in northwestern Ontario is one of the best-preserved ore-bearing calderas in the world. Sturgeon Lake Caldera formed about 2.7 billion years ago. Explosive felsic eruptions and submarine lava domes left nearly 3,000 m of fill inside it. Its Mattabi pyroclastic flow, a racing avalanche of hot ash and gas, is considered the third most voluminous eruptive event.

arch-062.title: Fossil raindrops weigh the ancient air
arch-062.text: Raindrops that fell 2.7 billion years ago left a measurement behind. Their fossil imprints in volcanic ash of South Africa's Ventersdorp Supergroup show air less than twice as dense as today's, likely similar or thinner. Gas bubbles in lava that set at sea level at the same time point to an air pressure of only 0.23 ± 0.23 bar. Both results contradict the idea that very high carbon dioxide or nitrogen kept the Archean warm under the faint young Sun.

arch-056.title: The Algoman orogeny builds the Superior Craton
arch-056.text:
The largest Archean craton on Earth was stitched together from many pieces. In the Algoman, or Kenoran, orogeny, repeated continental collisions, compression and subduction built mountains in the late Archean. Terranes now in the Canadian Shield collided about 2,700–2,500 million years ago, adding land along a belt from South Dakota to Sudbury, Ontario.

Between 2720 and 2680 million years ago, a run of these collisions assembled the Superior Craton. Subduction drove the docking, and dates of about 2,700 million years near Rainy Lake, Ontario, favor a model of moving plates. The orogeny closed the Archean about 2,500 million years ago. By then the continental crust was essentially formed, about 40 km thick.

arch-057.title: The oceans run short of nickel
arch-057.text: A shortage of one metal may have tipped the balance toward oxygen. From 2.7 to 2.4 billion years ago, nickel deposition fell steadily from 400 times today's level. Methane-making microbes need nickel. As volcanic nickel dwindled, oxygen producers began to outcompete them, and with fewer methane makers, less methane was left to soak up oxygen.

arch-063.title: Carbonate platforms grow in the Transvaal
arch-063.text: Microbes built limestone shelves the size of seas. Between about 2.640 and 2.516 billion years ago, two successive carbonate platforms, thick shelves of limy rock in shallow water, grew in the Transvaal Basin on the Kaapvaal craton. Stromatolites built them. The oldest known giant carbonate platform dates from about 2,600 million years ago, and a rising Transvaal sea flooded tidal flats about 2.550 billion years ago.

arch-064.title: The Great Dyke slices across Zimbabwe
arch-064.text: A ribbon of rock 550 km long runs straight across Zimbabwe. This Great Dyke is a band of layered ultramafic intrusions, 3–12 km wide, emplaced about 2.575 billion years ago. It has stayed undeformed since, showing that the craton had already stabilized. It holds major chromium and platinum resources, and it is one of the world's three most significant platinum sources.

arch-065.title: Arctica, a northern continent
arch-065.text: Siberia and Canada may once have shared one landmass. Arctica, a hypothetical continent, formed about 2.565 billion years ago from the Siberian, Slave, Wyoming, Superior and North Atlantic cratons. The {{ref:arch-056}} assembled it from the Canadian Shield and the Siberian craton. Rogers argued that it later rifted apart and reassembled along the 1.8-billion-year-old Trans-Hudson and Taltson-Thelon orogenies.

arch-066.title: Microbes begin to burn sulfur
arch-066.text: Some microbes learned to live by oxidizing sulfur, and they did it early. The earliest evidence, about 2.52 billion years old, comes from South Africa's Gamohaan Formation. It shows that sulfur-oxidizing bacteria evolved before the Great Oxygenation Event, while oxygen in the air was still scarce, drawing energy from sulfur compounds in their surroundings.

arch-067.title: An oxygen pulse closes the Archean
arch-067.text: The Archean ended with oxygen knocking at the door. Appreciable free oxygen was probably absent from the atmosphere until about 2,500 million years ago. Then, around 2,501 million years ago, a pulse of higher oxygen appeared, and some see it as a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event. The research is far from settled: studies from 2016–2022 put the onset anywhere from 2.7 to 2.3 billion years ago, including 2.501–2.434 billion.
